text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in Finnish newspapers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT

- Unemployment rose to 19 percent in December as the young rushed to register as job seekers ahead of tighter rules from turn of year. Labour Minister Liisa Jaakonsaari says high figure also shows labour market is now flexible.
- House prices are rising rapidly in good areas but still clearly below the peak in 1989. Current price increases are more selective than in 1980s. @
- There are 2.1 million licenced and about 100,000 illegal firearms in Finland -- over four guns per 10 Finns.
- Finland's national mediator Jorma Reini gets four-month probationary prison sentence for family violence and resisting police in December. Government due to sack him on Friday.
- Sweden's Telia plans to challenge Finnish mobile phone operators with city network due after the summer, official says.
- Foreign companies based in Finland are more profitable than Finnish firms due to more efficient use of capital, according to a study made by the Research Institute of the Finnish Economy (ETLA). @
KAUPPALEHTI
- Ten percent of Finland's exports are produced by foreign companies in Finland, ETLA study shows.
- Foreign ministry warns of problems in trade with Russia until Russia joins the World Trade Organisation.
- Swedish AssiDoman in talks to lease Karelian forests from Russia for 49 years. @
HUFVUDSTADSBLADET
- Finnish forest industry sceptical of planned pulp exchange due to start later this month.

- Finland now world leader in mobile phone density, with 130 percent growth in 1996. Telecom Finland official says slower growth pace in Sweden and Norway is due to the countries operators' strategy to subsidise handsets. @
DEMARI
- Security police chief Seppo Nevala fears that social changes might bring a threat to democratic structures from extremist groups.
AAMULEHTI
- A majority of Finns in poll support the present five-party government coalition and do not think that a proposal on liberalised opening hours should be an issue of confidence in parliament.
-- Helsinki Newsroom +358-9-680 50 242
